flashcards.back_definition: Input that is pasted into a database query gets read as SQL code, so the attacker can change what the query does.
flashcards.back_example: Typing ' OR '1'='1' -- into a login box makes the WHERE clause always true.
flashcards.back_confusion: Escaping HTML output stops XSS, not SQL injection; the fix for SQLi is parameterised queries.

flashcards.front: What is the main fix for SQL injection?
flashcards.back_definition: Parameterised queries (prepared statements): the query has placeholders and user input is passed separately, so it is always treated as data.
flashcards.back_confusion: A WAF and input validation help, but parameterisation is the primary control.

flashcards.front: What do UNION SELECT and the -- comment do in an injection?
flashcards.back_definition: UNION SELECT adds a second query to pull data from another table into the results; -- comments out the rest of the original query.
flashcards.back_example: ' UNION SELECT username, password FROM users --
flashcards.back_confusion: UNION only works when both queries return the same number of columns, so attackers probe for that first.
flashcards.back_hook: Join their query on; comment yours off.

flashcards.back_definition: Injection where the page shows no query results, so the attacker learns data indirectly: from true/false page differences or deliberate time delays.
flashcards.back_example: If the first letter of the admin password is 'a', sleep 5 seconds.
flashcards.back_confusion: No visible output does not mean no vulnerability.
flashcards.back_hook: Asking yes/no questions, one character at a time.

flashcards.back_definition: Injecting script into a page so it runs in other users' browsers, with their session and permissions.
flashcards.back_example: A forum comment containing .
flashcards.back_confusion: XSS attacks the site's users, while SQL injection attacks its database.
flashcards.back_hook: The site serves the attacker's code to its own visitors.

flashcards.front: Reflected vs stored vs DOM-based XSS?
flashcards.back_definition: Reflected: the payload comes in the request (often a crafted link) and is echoed back. Stored: it is saved on the server and served to every viewer. DOM-based: the page's own JavaScript writes untrusted data into the page without it reaching the server.
flashcards.back_example: The 2005 Samy worm was stored XSS on MySpace and added over a million friends within a day.
flashcards.back_confusion: Stored XSS needs no special link, so it can hit everyone who views the page.
flashcards.back_hook: Bounced, saved, or built in the browser.

flashcards.back_definition: Encoding output for its context (HTML, attribute, JavaScript, URL) so special characters show as text, backed by a Content Security Policy.
flashcards.back_example: < becomes <, so <script> is displayed instead of run.
flashcards.back_confusion: Blocking the word <script> fails: onerror=, javascript: links and SVG still work.

flashcards.back_definition: Broken object-level authorisation: an API returns or changes an object by its ID without checking that the caller is allowed to access that specific object.
flashcards.back_example: Changing /api/orders/1001 to /api/orders/1002 shows someone else's order.
flashcards.back_confusion: It is an authorisation failure, not an authentication failure: the attacker is logged in, just not entitled.
flashcards.back_hook: Logged in is not the same as allowed.

flashcards.front: What is excessive data exposure in an API?
flashcards.back_definition: The server sends more fields than the client needs and relies on the front-end to hide them.
flashcards.back_example: The profile API returns date of birth and password-reset tokens; the app just doesn't display them.
flashcards.back_confusion: Hiding data or buttons in the UI does nothing; attackers call the API directly with curl or Postman.
flashcards.back_hook: If the server sends it, the attacker has it.

flashcards.back_definition: An endpoint meant for admins can be called by any logged-in user because the server never checks the role.
flashcards.back_example: A student calls POST /api/admin/grades and it works.
flashcards.back_confusion: Every endpoint must check permission on the server, not just hide the menu item.
flashcards.back_hook: Check the role at the door, not on the map.

flashcards.front: What makes one data breach worse than another?
flashcards.back_definition: The type of data (health, financial, ID numbers, credentials), how many records, and how long it took to detect and contain.
flashcards.back_example: 40 patients' health records can be more serious than 4 million newsletter emails.
flashcards.back_confusion: A breach with no passwords can still enable identity theft and carry strict notification duties.

flashcards.back_definition: PII is personally identifiable information (name, address, ID numbers, date of birth). PHI is protected health information, regulated in the US by HIPAA.
flashcards.back_example: A patient's name plus diagnosis is PHI.
flashcards.back_confusion: PHI is a subset of sensitive personal data with extra legal rules; breach notification laws apply to both.
flashcards.back_hook: PII says who; PHI says who and what's wrong with them.

flashcards.front: How did Equifax get breached in 2017?
flashcards.back_definition: Attackers exploited an Apache Struts flaw (CVE-2017-5638) that had a patch available two months earlier, then took data on about 147 million people.
flashcards.back_example: The fix was released in March; the attackers got in from mid-May.
flashcards.back_confusion: It was a known, patchable flaw: a patch-management failure, not a zero-day.
flashcards.back_hook: The patch was there; nobody applied it.
